prompt: I run Kilnroom, a ceramics studio in Tacoma that ships a box of three handmade mugs or bowls every other month ($64 a box, skip or cancel anytime). Need a homepage for it. Single self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts only, no external images or scripts. Use placeholder blocks where photos would go. People mostly arrive from Instagram on their phones but my partner will look at it on a laptop.
rubric: At the first screen of a laptop-width render, a visitor can tell what Kilnroom sells, roughly what it costs, and where to act, without scrolling.
The page is paced as a sequence of distinct sections that do different jobs (for example what arrives, how it works, who makes it, a closing ask) rather than the same card row repeated.
Photo placeholders are given real size and position in the composition, so the page already reads as having imagery rather than a stack of text blocks.
Text blocks that run more than a line or two stay at a comfortable reading width rather than stretching across the whole laptop viewport.
At phone width the page reads as one coherent column in a sensible order with no horizontal scroll and no clipped content.

prompt: Can you build the page for one section of our docs? The tool is called Brine, a command line backup utility. Page is 'Restoring a snapshot'. It should have the usual docs navigation (about 12 pages across 3 groups: Getting started, Backups, Reference), the article itself with an intro, 4 numbered steps with a code block each, a warning about restoring over existing files, and a 'Next steps' bit at the end. Make up the content, keep it believable. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external anything. It'll be used mostly on laptops and sometimes on a phone.
rubric: Navigation, article and any secondary element (such as an on-page outline) are clearly separated into regions, and the article is visibly the dominant one.
Article prose sits in a column of comfortable line length, not the full width left over after the navigation.
Code blocks are not squeezed into the prose measure in a way that forces constant sideways scrolling for ordinary commands, and they scroll or wrap inside their own box rather than breaking the page.
The navigation lines up with the content below it: groups are labelled, the current page is evident, and the nav does not float disconnected from the article's top edge.
At phone width the navigation collapses or moves out of the way so the article is still the first thing read, with nothing overflowing the viewport.

prompt: Our new product listing page for Tallow & Bolt (hardware and fixings, about 1,800 SKUs) went live last week and conversions on category pages are down. Here's how it's built: a full-width dark banner at the top, 180px tall, with the category name and a paragraph about our delivery promise. Under it, a filter sidebar on the left with 14 collapsible filter groups, all expanded by default, so it's about four screens long. Then a product grid at 6 across on a 1440 screen: each card is a small square photo, the name, and the price, and nothing else. Pagination at the bottom, 24 per page. On a phone the sidebar is just stacked above the grid. What's wrong with the structure and what would you change? Don't redo the visual style, I mean the layout.
rubric: Identifies that the filter column competes with or buries the products, especially on a phone where the grid is pushed below a very long filter stack.

Questions the density or card count of the grid: names a concrete problem with six small cards (too little information per product to decide, or too small to read) and gives a different column count or card content.
Notes that the banner and delivery paragraph consume the first screen without helping someone choose a product, and says what the first screen should show instead.
Gives concrete structural changes (what collapses, what moves, what the phone layout becomes) rather than generic advice like 'improve hierarchy' or 'add whitespace'.
Stays on layout and structure and does not spend its answer on colors, fonts or restyling, as the user asked.

prompt: Working on the settings area for Driftline, a fleet tracking web app for small delivery companies. There are about 40 settings: company profile, billing and invoices, team members and roles, vehicles and drivers, alert rules, notification channels, integrations (6 of them), data export, and a few security things. Our designer wants a left sidebar with every group, our dev wants one long page with anchor links, and the PM wants top tabs. Which should we do? I need a pick, not a survey, and what the screen looks like on a laptop and on a phone.
rubric: Commits to one structure and says why in terms of this app's content (the number of groups, how different they are, how people arrive at them).
Describes the laptop layout concretely enough to build from: where navigation lives, how wide the content area is, and what a single group's page looks like.
Describes a different, workable phone layout rather than assuming the laptop structure shrinks unchanged.
Addresses what happens with the groups that are much larger than the rest (such as team members or integrations) instead of treating all 40 settings as the same kind of thing.
Briefly says why the rejected options lose for this case rather than ignoring them.

prompt: We're putting on a poetry night: 'Low Tide Readings', Friday 14 November, 7:30pm, at the Harbor Street Boathouse, free entry, four readers, with a short open mic after. I need that one message to go out as an A3 portrait poster, a square Instagram post, a 9:16 story, and a wide banner for the top of the event page (about 1600 x 400). Don't make the art, just tell me how each version should be laid out: what goes where, what's biggest, what gets dropped or moved in each format. Short and practical.
rubric: Gives a distinct arrangement for each of the four formats, not the same stack of text restated four times.
Identifies the one thing each format must establish first (the event name and date, say) and keeps it dominant across all four.
The wide banner is arranged horizontally (text and image side by side or a single line of information) and does not simply stretch the poster into a short strip.
States what is dropped or reduced in the small and tall formats (such as the reader list, the open mic note or the full address) and what stays.
Accounts for the vertical story format's unsafe edges or the poster's viewing distance in at least one place instead of ignoring where the format will actually be seen.

prompt: I'm planning the landing page for Ledgerlark, bookkeeping software for freelance electricians and plumbers. Features: snap a receipt and it's categorised, mileage tracking from the phone, quarterly tax estimate, invoices with card payment, and a bank feed. Pricing is $12 a month, 30-day free trial. We have 3 customer quotes, a short demo video, and a comparison with doing it in a spreadsheet. I have a lot to say and I'm afraid it will turn into a wall of boxes. Plan the page for me: the sequence of sections, what the top of the page has to do, and how it should vary in rhythm so it doesn't feel like the same block repeated.
rubric: Proposes a specific ordered list of sections with a stated job for each, rather than a generic landing page template.
Defines the first screen concretely: what is stated, what is shown and what the single next action is.
Does not give all five features equal weight in equal blocks; it picks a lead feature or groups the rest, and says how the sections differ in shape or density.
Places the proof (quotes, demo, comparison) at sensible points in the sequence instead of dumping them together at the end.
Includes at least one place where the pattern deliberately changes (a full-width moment, a quote, a switch from text-led to visual-led) so the page has a pace.

prompt: My sister is getting married and wants a simple page for guests: names (Ines & Tomás), 20 June, the chapel at Quinta do Moinho, the schedule (ceremony 4pm, drinks 5:30, dinner 7:30, dancing till late), how to get there, a dress code note, and an RSVP button that goes to a form somewhere else (just link to #rsvp). Nothing fancy. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no images or external anything.
rubric: Page reads as a calm single-column page that suits the occasion; it is not turned into a multi-column marketing layout with feature cards, a sidebar or a dense grid.
The names and date are the clear opening of the first screen, and the RSVP action is easy to find without hunting.
Schedule is easy to scan as a sequence of times and events, not buried in a paragraph.
The column is a comfortable reading width on a wide screen and does not stretch edge to edge, with the content centered or deliberately placed.
Works on a phone with no horizontal scroll, and the information is in a sensible order for a guest planning their day.

prompt: About to ship the article template for our newsletter archive (Saltworks Weekly) and I'd like a last look at the layout. Here's the structure: the page has a slim top bar with the logo on the left and 'Subscribe' on the right. Below it, the article is a single column 66 characters wide centered on the page, with the headline, a one-line standfirst, author and date, then body text at 18px with generous line height. Subheads break the text every 300 words or so, and pull quotes are allowed to extend about 80px into the margins on desktop. Images are the same width as the text, except the lead image, which runs wider than the text column. A small 'More from this issue' list sits after the article, then a subscribe box and a footer. On phones everything is one column with 20px side padding. Anything you'd change before it ships? Be honest, if it's fine just say so.
rubric: Concludes that the layout is fundamentally sound and ready to ship, rather than finding a problem for every part of it.
Does not recommend replacing the single-column structure with a multi-column, sidebar or grid layout.
Any changes proposed are few (about three or fewer), small, and specific, and they are presented as optional polish rather than required fixes.
Names at least one thing that works and why (for example the measure, the controlled breaks from the column, or the order of what follows the article).
Does not ask for a redesign, new features or additional sections that the user did not mention.

prompt: Quick one. Portfolio site for a freelance illustrator. Should the first screen be one huge full-bleed illustration with the name small in the corner, or a smaller image with her name and a line about what she does next to it? Answer in three sentences max, I'm just deciding.
rubric: Gives one clear recommendation, not a both-ways answer.
The whole answer is three sentences or fewer.
The reason given ties to what a first-time visitor needs to understand on arrival, or to what the work looks like, rather than being a generic statement.
Does not add a bulleted list, headers, or a follow-up menu of alternatives.

prompt: Build me the opening of a long-read feature for our regional magazine, the kind of page where the story starts big. Title: 'The Last Salt Barge'. Subtitle-ish line: 'On the Medway, one family keeps a trade alive that the tide stopped paying for.' By Rhea Okonkwo-Hale, 22 minutes. Photo credit goes with the lead image (use a placeholder block for the photo). Then the first four paragraphs of the story, which you can make up, about 90 words each. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, nothing external. It should feel like a magazine, not a blog post.
rubric: The opening makes a composed first screen where the title and the lead image are a single arrangement, not a headline stacked above an unrelated block.
There is a visible change of scale or placement between the opening (title, image) and the running text, so the page has an entrance before the reading starts.
Body paragraphs sit at a comfortable reading measure and are clearly separated from the display elements.
Byline, reading time and photo credit are present and placed deliberately (for example grouped and aligned to something) rather than scattered.
At phone width the opening still works as a composition in a single column, with the image and title in a sensible order and no overflow.
